Performers
Adèle Bérard (soprano), Laura Lazayre (piano) Documented

The Commons description lists duo Béla with Adèle Bérard, soprano, and Laura Lazayre, piano. The ICCARE programme lists the same duo’s recital with the pianist’s surname spelt Lazayres; no other source for the spelling was found, and the Commons spelling, which appears on all three files the uploader posted, is kept. The file is credited to the uploader Magiraud as own work; the page does not name the uploader as a performer.

[1] [5]
Work version
Complete song as printed in Op. 1 No. 3, sung in the printed key (A minor), with the repeat of the last line Inferred, not documented

The Commons title and description identify the song, and the page links the OpenScore Lieder project as the score; its transcription of this song is a CC0 encoding made from the Bote & Bock first edition (IMSLP #99178). That the performance is complete, untransposed and follows the printed repeat is estimated from the audio and the printed score: the piano’s opening E5 measures 659.6 Hz, the soprano’s first notes sound as A4 and E5, the closing chord is A minor, and audio chroma aligned with the encoded score follows four stanzas in printed order and then the repeated last line. Tuning is about A = 440 Hz. The sung words were not transcribed. IMSLP gives the key as A minor and the first edition marks the song Andante (p. 9). The Naxos booklet, LiederNet and the chronological work list after Hellwig-⁠Unruh’s catalogue date the song 1837; IMSLP and the first edition place its publication in 1846, the year Hensel told her brother Felix that she had accepted Herr Bock’s offer (letter of 9 July 1846).

Recorded
22 January 2026 Documented

The Commons date field gives 2026-01-22, and the ICCARE programme places the duo’s recital, billed “avec captation libre”, on Thursday 22 January from 18:00 to 19:00. The Commons description gives 22–⁠23 January, the span of the conference days. The page does not say whether the file records the public recital or another run-through on the same day. The upload timestamp, 23 January 2026 at 09:08 UTC, is not a session date.

[1] [5]
Place
Logis du Roy, Amiens, France Documented

The ICCARE programme places the conference days, with the recital, at the Logis du Roy, Passage du Logis du Roy, Amiens. The coordinates on the Commons page (49.89292 N, 2.299879 E) coincide with the OpenStreetMap building “Logis du Roi” (49.89292 N, 2.29988 E). The room is not named.

[1] [5] [6]
Transfer
Audio track extracted by Contrapunctus from the Wikimedia Commons video “Warum sind denn die Rosen so blass – Fanny Mendelssohn, Heinrich Heine.webm” (uploaded by Magiraud, own work), with ffmpeg -vn -ac 2 -ar 44100 -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 160k, adding ID3v2.3 tags for title, performers, licence and the Commons page. Original file SHA-256 ba5c6b2dffda834c3d41fd03ae8f39a072ca5dad282b48124cd360e3ea8bc772; derived MP3 SHA-256 e9185202a46df85a80963accd1ac574d478500b12a73f2b5351b2f9a62388130. Documented

Commons offers this file only as video, with no MP3 derivative, so the site hosts the audio-only MP3 itself at assets/audio/fanny-hensel-warum-rosen.mp3. The SHA-1 of the cached original, e876d1fce86fb1a0c80e13fee6d12908b47689e5, equals the SHA-1 on the Commons file page. The tool removes the container metadata (-map_metadata -1) and writes its own attribution tags.

[1] [2] [3]
Transfer date
2026-10-19 Documented

Date of the extraction by Contrapunctus, from the time stamps of the cached original and the MP3. The Commons upload on 23 January 2026 is not a transfer date.

[3]
Processing
Video stream removed; the Vorbis audio (48 kHz, stereo) was decoded and re-encoded as MP3 at 160 kb/s, 44.1 kHz, stereo (libmp3lame). No trimming, level change, equalisation or noise reduction was applied. Documented

The original is a WebM file of 99,950,566 bytes with VP8 video (1920 × 1080) and Vorbis audio, 141.2 s long; the MP3 decodes to 141.1 s. Microphones, the recording chain, editing and mastering before upload are not documented.

[2] [3]
Composition rights
Public domain: Hensel died in 1847 and Heine in 1856, and the first edition appeared in 1846. Inferred, not documented

Life-plus-70 terms have run out for both authors, and IMSLP lists the 1846 Bote & Bock edition as public domain. This covers the song and its text, not modern editions; the OpenScore Lieder transcription is released under CC0.

[8] [11]
Recording rights
CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons file licence). The audio-only MP3 derived by Contrapunctus is distributed under the same licence. Documented

Attribution is required to duo Béla (Adèle Bérard and Laura Lazayre) and to the uploader, Magiraud; the share-alike term passes the licence to the derivative, and the changes (video removed, audio re-encoded) are stated in the credit line. The licence is the uploader’s own-work declaration, and the Commons page carries no separate statement or permission ticket from the performers. The ICCARE programme, which announces the recital as “avec captation libre” at a conference on open licences and open data, points to an open release but gives no licence terms. Nothing on the Commons or ICCARE pages contradicts the own-work claim.

Fanny Hensel, Warum sind denn die Rosen so blass (Heine), Sechs Lieder, Op. 1 No. 3. Adèle Bérard, soprano, and Laura Lazayre, piano (duo Béla); recorded on 22 January 2026 at the ICCARE days “Science ouverte, données ouvertes et musique”, Logis du Roy, Amiens. Video uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Magiraud (own work), CC BY-SA 4.0; audio-only MP3 extracted by Contrapunctus (video removed, audio re-encoded at 160 kb/s) and distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0. The composition is in the public domain. Rights statement
